data.text/html:
Intro to Linear Programming: the carpenter's problem

An interactive companion to Dr. Trefor Bazett's video "Intro to Linear Programming". A carpenter can build tables or bookcases, with a limited supply of wood and time. How many of each should they make to earn the most money? We answer this with no calculus and no matrices, only a picture: shade a region, slide a line across it, and look where the line touches last.

data.text/markdown:
Colour language used throughout

colour meaning
■ orange the labour constraint ||(5x+4y\le 80||) (hours)
■ brown the lumber constraint ||(10x+20y\le 200||) (wood)
■ green the feasible region, i.e. plans that break no rule (green, like in the video)
■ blue iso-value lines, where profit ||(180x+200y||) is constant
■ red the optimum
■ purple your plan or guess

1 · What is a linear program?

Despite the name, programming here means planning, not coding. A linear program is ||[\text{optimize}\quad 180x + 200y \qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \begin{cases}5x + 4y \le 80\\ 10x + 20y \le 200\\ x \ge 0,\; y \ge 0\end{cases}||]Everything is linear: no ||(x^2||), no ||(\sin x||), only numbers times variables, added up. "Optimize" can mean maximize or minimize.

The carpenter problem

lumber (units) labour (hours) profit
table (||(x||)) 10 5 $180
bookcase (||(y||)) 20 4 $200
available 200 80 maximize
So ||(x||) tables use ||(10x||) lumber and ||(5x||) hours, and ||(y||) bookcases use ||(20y||) lumber and ||(4y||) hours. Before reading on, pick a production plan. Can you beat $3,000?

data.text/markdown:
2 · Graphing inequalities: the feasible region

Each inequality is a line plus a side. The line ||(5x+4y=80||) is "all 80 hours used exactly", and ||(5x+4y\le 80||) shades everything beneath it. Do this for every constraint: the spot where all shadings overlap (dark green in the video) is the feasible region. ||[\underbrace{5x+4y\le 80}_{\text{labour}}\ \cap\ \underbrace{10x+20y\le 200}_{\text{lumber}}\ \cap\ \underbrace{x\ge0,\ y\ge0}_{\text{no negative furniture}}||]Four edges give a quadrilateral with four vertices. Any point inside it is a legal plan. Drag the purple dot (or click anywhere) to test plans. Use the sliders to change the carpenter's budgets.

data.text/markdown:
3 · Computing the maximum: check the corners

The video's intuition: if you finish with unused wood or unused hours, you could have built more and earned more. So the best plan should use all of both, which is the vertex where the two lines cross. Turn both inequalities into equations: ||[5x+4y=80 \;\Rightarrow\; y = 20-\tfrac54x \qquad\qquad 10x+20y=200 \;\Rightarrow\; y = 10-\tfrac{x}{2}||]||[20-\tfrac54x = 10-\tfrac x2 \;\Rightarrow\; x=\tfrac{40}{3}\approx 13.3,\quad y=\tfrac{10}{3}\approx 3.33,\quad 180x+200y \approx \$3{,}066.67||]The general recipe: intersect every pair of boundary lines, throw away crossings that break a rule, and evaluate the profit at the survivors. Step through it below. Green dots are kept, red ✗s are infeasible crossings, and the red star is the best so far. Note: one slide in the video writes the lumber rule as 10x + 10y ≤ 200 and says the all-bookcase corner pays $1,800. The setup (20 lumber per bookcase) gives 10x + 20y ≤ 200 and 200·10 = $2,000 there. The optimum ($3,066.67) is unaffected.

data.text/markdown:
4 · Iso-value lines: why the answer is a corner

That still leaves a question: why must the best plan be a vertex? The video's argument uses iso-value lines, which are all plans that earn the same amount ||(c||): ||[180x + 200y = c||]Changing ||(c||) slides the line parallel to itself. A bigger ||(c||) moves it up and to the right, in the direction of the arrow ||((180, 200)||), which points where profit grows fastest.
  • Is ||(c||) too big? The line misses the green region, so no feasible plan earns that much.
  • Is ||(c||) too small? Lots of feasible plans earn it, but you're leaving money on the table.
  • The best ||(c||) is the largest one where the line still "comes down and kisses" the region. For a polygon, that kiss happens at a vertex.
Drag on the plane to sweep the blue line (it follows your pointer). Drag the arrow tip to change the profit per table or bookcase.

data.text/markdown:
5 · The big idea, and when it breaks

If the feasible region is a bounded, convex polygon, a linear function reaches its maximum and its minimum at a vertex.
So the method is: list the vertices, evaluate, pick the best. The video adds two caveats, and there is one more worth knowing:
  • Ties: if the iso-line is parallel to an edge, the whole edge is optimal (its end vertices included).
  • Minimum: the same picture works. Slide the line down until it last touches. For the carpenter that's ||(c = 0||) at ||((0,0)||).
  • Unbounded: if the region runs off to infinity in the arrow's direction, no maximum exists. The "vertices only" rule needs the region to be bounded.
Pick a case. Each one uses the same iso-line widget; press snap to optimum.

data.text/markdown:
6 · Sandbox: write your own linear program

Edit the constraint table (each row means ||(a\,x + b\,y \le r||); for a "≥" rule, multiply by −1), set the objective, and the region, vertices and iso-line all update. Rows with a = b = 0 are ignored.

Recap

idea in symbols what you did
linear program optimize ||(px+qy||) subject to ||(a_ix+b_iy\le r_i||) turned the carpenter story into ||(180x+200y||), ||(5x+4y\le80||), ||(10x+20y\le200||)
feasible region intersection of half-planes (a convex polygon) dragged a plan point and read off slack
vertices crossings of two boundary lines that satisfy every rule stepped through all ||(\binom{m}{2}||) crossings
iso-value line ||(px+qy=c||), slides parallel as ||(c||) changes swept ||(c||) until the line kissed the region
big idea bounded region ⇒ max & min at a vertex carpenter optimum ||((40/3,\,10/3)||), $3,066.67
caveats ties (parallel edge), minimize, unbounded explored each in section 5
Next steps: the simplex method (hop vertex → better neighbour rather than checking all of them), integer programming (the carpenter can't sell a third of a table: the best whole-number plan is (12, 4) for $2,960, not the rounded (13, 3) at $2,940, and you can check it in section 1), and duality (what is one more hour of labour worth?).
